essay.title: Thirty seconds
essay.prompt_text: The lessons we take from obstacles we encounter can be fundamental to later success. Recount a time when you faced a challenge, setback, or failure. How did it affect you, and what did you learn from the experience?
essay.body:
For the first thirty seconds of every FTC match, nobody is allowed to touch the robot. It runs on whatever code you gave it, and you just stand behind the line and watch.

At our first qualifier sophomore year, I watched our robot drive straight past the scoring zone and into the wall. Then it did it again the next match. I had written that autonomous routine, and I had tested it in our practice room maybe fifty times. Every time it worked. On the real field it didn't, and I had no idea why.

On the bus home I kept replaying it. I had been so sure the code was right that I never wrote down what I changed between tests. When something broke, I fixed it from memory and moved on. So when it failed at the qualifier, I had nothing to look back at. I couldn't even tell which version was running.

The team decided to rebuild the whole autonomous program from scratch, and everyone stayed late every night that week.

The next Monday I started a log. Every test got a line: the date, the battery level, what I changed, and what the robot actually did. It was boring. Some nights the log said the same thing ten times in a row. But after two weeks the pattern was obvious. Our practice room had carpet tiles, the competition field had foam mats, and the wheels slipped just enough on the foam that every turn came up short. The code was never wrong. My idea of where the robot was standing was wrong.

We fixed it by having the robot check its position with a sensor instead of trusting how far the wheels had turned. At the state championship that spring, our autonomous scored in every match, and the judges gave us the Think Award for our engineering notebook, which was mostly my log, cleaned up.

I learned a lot about perseverance and teamwork that season.

I think about that log on Saturdays now, at the Code Club I started at the library. When one of the middle schoolers says their Scratch game is broken, the old me would have grabbed the mouse and fixed it. Now I ask them what they expected to happen and what happened instead, and we write it on a sticky note. Usually they find the bug before I do. One girl kept a stack of sticky notes on her laptop for a month, then started her own log in a notebook with a dinosaur on the cover.

Being wrong in front of everyone is not fun. But I would rather find out exactly how I was wrong than be right by accident. That is why I want to study computer science.

Interviewer: Let's start with FIRST Tech Challenge team. What was your own role on the team?

Student: I wrote the autonomous code for our robot and now I teach the new kids Java.

Interviewer: Got it, so you own the robot's code and train the new members. Next, Code Club for middle schoolers. What's your part in it?

Student: I started a free coding club at the library because my little cousin had nowhere to learn.

Interviewer: So you founded it. About how many hours a week do you spend on Code Club for middle schoolers?
